entries.title: White Sox officially retire Ozzie Guillen's No. 13
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> retired <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/03/white-sox-ozzie-guillen-retire-number-13" target="_blank" >Ozzie Guillen’s No. 13</a> on Saturday night.</p><p>There were laughs, some gentle roasts, memories, emotional moments, recollections of 2005 and mentions of family.</p><p>Guillen’s speech even went long, and the Sox’ game against the Guardians started 17 minutes after it was scheduled.</p><p>So, yes, the event perfectly captured Guillen.</p><p>The manager of the Sox’ 2005 World Series champions, Guillen has come to embody the team. He played for them for 13 seasons, managed them for eight mostly successful (but occasionally explosive) years and has become a beloved and honest TV analyst.</p><p>‘‘Isn’t that like the ultimate thing, to be able to be all three of those things for one team?’’ former Sox catcher A.J. Pierzynski told the Sun-Times. ‘‘He’s really lived the dream of any baseball player with one organization.’’</p><p>Guillen has done that despite — and partially because of — his honesty.</p><p>Blunt as a manager and even more forthright as an analyst, Guillen says what he’s thinking. At times, that got him in trouble with the media and contributed to his stint as the manager of the Marlins lasting only a season.</p><p>It’s also something his former Sox players and today’s fans appreciate about him.</p><p>‘‘He literally told you what he was expecting out of you or what he thought of you,’’ former Sox pitcher Mark Buehrle said. ‘‘Whether it was good or bad, you might not have wanted to hear it, but his door was always open. You could walk in at any time. You might not want to hear what he’s going to tell you, but he’s going to tell you the truth.’’</p><p>Sometimes, however, that can lead to bad exits.</p><p>Guillen and then-vice president Ken Williams saw their professional relationship blow up in 2011. Six years after winning a World Series together, Guillen left for Miami to end one of the most productive and tempestuous partnerships in Chicago baseball.</p><p>But time can change perspectives. Guillen looked back thankfully on Williams hiring him before the 2004 season. Guillen, who replaced the laid-back Jerry Manuel, turned 40 that winter and was selected despite his youth and relative inexperience.</p><p>That decision changed the Sox’ trajectory. And Guillen’s life.</p><p>Guillen became the first manager to lead the Sox to multiple postseason appearances and in 2005 joined a small list of Chicago managers and coaches to win a championship, securing his place in the city’s history.</p><p>‘‘I know there were a lot of ups and downs, hate and love,’’ Guillen said. ‘‘Beautiful, nice but ugly, but we got it done. I did everything in my power in my life to make the White Sox team win every day.’’</p><p>As a player and a manager — and even as an analyst — another one of Guillen’s most defining traits is his emotion. He mostly kept that in check Saturday, with a couple of<br>notable exceptions.</p><p>Venezuela has been bruised and beaten by political forces and natural disasters, and Guillen included his home country in the celebration. In conjunction with the festivities, the Sox and Guillen launched the Relief for Venezuela fundraiser to benefit earthquake recovery and relief.</p><p>Wearing pins of the Venezuelan flag on his lapel, Guillen beamed when he spoke about the country’s baseball heritage and how many of its greats wear or wore No. 13. Dave Concepcion, the shortstop for the 1970s ‘‘Big Red Machine’’ that won the 1975 and 1976 World Series, donned No. 13. The Braves’ Ronald Acuna Jr. wears it now.</p><p>No Sox figure will wear it again. The No. 13 is now on display above the first-base line, next to the No. 11 worn by Hall of Fame shortstop and fellow Venezuelan legend Luis Aparicio.</p><p>Aparicio’s son Nelson — yes, named for his father’s longtime double-play partner, Nellie Fox — was visibly stirred when the curtain hiding Guillen’s name and number came down.</p><p>‘‘It’s a dream,’’ Nelson Aparicio told the Sun-Times after watching the ceremony on the field next to the Sox’ third-base dugout. ‘‘Seeing his name besides my father’s name, that’s great. Two Venezuelans from the same organization with their number retired.’’</p><p>Guillen was just glad to live to see his number go up.</p><p>It’s hard to know whether he was joking, but Guillen said that when the topic came up, he would tell his wife, Ibis, that the team was just waiting until he died to retire his No. 13. More seriously, he relished the fact that chairman Jerry Reinsdorf is still around and that former broadcaster Ken ‘‘Hawk’’ Harrelson is, too.</p><p>Then here’s where the emotions really kicked in for Guillen.</p><p>‘‘I’m going to look up and see the last name every day,’’ Guillen said. ‘‘To me, the biggest thrill when I see the number [and] the name out there is what it means to my grandkids to walk to this field and see that. That’s the biggest thrill to me.’’</p><p>Tearing up, Guillen then said he would stop talking about his kids and family to keep himself from crying.</p>

entries.title: ‘We’ve got tired players’ at close of 17 games in 17 days, but Cubs have thrived during challenging stretch
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY – <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> is perhaps baseball’s best defender.</p><p>But for the second time in four games, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/05/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-shohei-ohtani-nl-mvp-race-dodgers-playoffs-craig-counsell-shota-imanaga" >MVP candidate</a> was not in his usual spot center field but DH’ing, off his feet once more as the team comes to the end of a stretch of 17 games in 17 days.</p><p>“We’ve got tired players, for sure,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said before Saturday’s game, a 6-3 loss to the Royals.</p><p>It’s a daunting stretch for any team, but in the face of such a physical challenge, the Cubs have thrived, going 11-5 with one game remaining before Monday’s off day.</p><p>The Cubs came into Saturday tops in the NL with a .770 OPS, 144 hits and 81 runs scored since the stretch began July 24.</p><p>Their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/30/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-pitching-starting-rotation-matthew-boyd-shota-imanaga-colin-rea-david-peterson-javier-assad-tarik-skubal" >starting pitching was particularly impressive</a>, with a 2.65 ERA that ranked second in the NL. Remove <b>Jameson Taillon</b>’s seven-run clunker in his final game with the Cubs, and that number was down to 2.03, second best in baseball.</p><p>In the thick of it all, the Cubs went through an eventful trade deadline, which saw <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >an aggressive front office</a> try to best position them for a deep October run, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/04/cubs-dodgers-three-peat-world-series-favorites-tarik-skubal-dansby-swanson" >a raucous sweep of the juggernaut Dodgers</a>.</p><p>“This was 17 in a row. For most teams, that’s their longest stretch of the season,” Counsell said. “It happened at a time in the season where the trade deadline’s around it, which creates a lot around the team. Some hot weather in multiple cities that you play in, you always worry about it.</p><p>“We’ve handled the first 15 games exceptionally well, especially our starting pitching has been outstanding for this stretch and, to me, the key to this. That’s what can go wrong in [a stretch like this] more than anything, [impacting the bullpen], and they’ve been excellent.”</p><p><b>Happ gets ahold of one</b></p><p>Left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> has been struggling at the plate, coming into Saturday hitting just .162 with a sub-.300 on-base percentage and only one home run in his previous 34 games. A four-strikeout game Friday was particularly ugly.</p><p>But he got off the schneid Saturday, snapping an 0-for-22 stretch at the dish by homering for the first time since July 20, later adding a double.</p><p>“For us to be the best team we can be,” Counsell said before the game, “we need Ian Happ to be a good player.”</p><p>That the dinger came off a righty won’t make his splits any less dramatic; he came into Saturday with a .798 OPS against right-handers versus a .517 OPS against left-handers.</p><p>But it was a positive result for an important Cubs hitter.</p><p>“A very good night, he’ll sleep good,” Counsell said after the game. “Hopefully, we’re getting the good Ian back. It’s been frustrating for him, but this is a good hitter, this is a guy who’s having a good year against right-handed pitching. He’s going to do good things for us.”</p><p><b>Holmes rusty in return</b></p><p>Newly acquired right-hander <b>Clay Holmes</b> made his Cubs debut Saturday, his first time on a major league mound since May 15, when he went on the injured list with a fractured fibula.</p><p>It didn’t go too great, with Holmes tagged for four runs in four innings of work.</p><p>A brief outing was not entirely unexpected, given the long layoff.</p><p>“It took a lot of work to get back to this point, and it definitely felt good to be back in a big league game,” Holmes said. “Obviously, that’s not the full goal. You want to be back and helping this team win games. I just wasn’t quite sharp enough tonight.”</p>

entries.title: Family of man whose body was at South Chicago Chapel told his body can be released
entries.summary: <p>As the Cook County medical examiner’s office works to identify the 56 bodies removed from a South Side funeral home, the family of Keith Allen Young learned Saturday his body can be released, his sister said.</p><p>The update brings Young’s family a step closer to paying their respects. His body, which they thought was being prepared by South Chicago Chapel for burial, never arrived at the church for his wake on Thursday.</p><p>Young's funeral was supposed to be Friday. Instead, his family went to the medical examiner’s office to see what they could find out.</p><p>Stephanie Young said the medical examiner’s office contacted one of her brothers Saturday to say their brother's body had been identified. She believes the next step is for the family to find another funeral home that can receive her brother’s body.</p><p>“It’s just the devastation to our family to have to redo this whole situation over again,” Young said. “At this point, we’re just happy to have his body ... so we can move forward in laying him to rest.”</p><p>Keith Allen Young, 48, died July 26. His body <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/07/south-side-funeral-home-bodies-families-investigation" target="_blank" ><u>was delivered</u></a> Wednesday to South Chicago Chapel, 2939 E. 95th St., the same day the business had its license revoked, as previously reported by the Sun-Times.</p><p>The funeral home was supposed to prepare his body and deliver it to a church Thursday, but it never arrived.</p><p>Young’s relatives said their calls to the funeral home seeking answers were not returned, and the family learned through the media that the funeral home had been shut down.</p><p>The medical examiner’s office said Friday it had taken jurisdiction of 56 remains from the funeral home and was working to assess their condition, confirm identification and ensure appropriate paperwork was filed.</p><p>The office could not confirm Saturday how many of the remains had been identified so far or provide additional updates on the process.</p><p>Additional information was expected Monday morning, according to Natalia Derevyanny, spokesperson for the medical examiner’s office.</p><p>Young's bodies and others were found on Thursday by police. Officers went to the chapel that day learning that bodies at the South Deering funeral home were not being stored at or below 40 degrees, as required by state regulations, according to a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times. Inside, officers found dozens of bodies in various areas of the funeral home. The bodies were not refrigerated and were in various stages of decomposition, according to the report.<br></p>

entries.title: Sophie Cunningham draws dueling protests outside Sky-Fever game
entries.summary: <p>Here was the scene outside the United Center on Saturday: On one side of Madison Street, a group had gathered to “Support Sophie,” with a cardboard cutout of Fever guard <b>Sophie Cunningham</b> and T-shirts bearing XX and XY chromosomes.</p><p>A few yards away, counterprotesters waved rainbow and transgender flags and wore shirts reading “Protect Trans Kids.”</p><p>Why outside a Fever-<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> game?</p><p>Cunningham has become a flashpoint in the debate over transgender participation in women’s sports. In an ESPN profile, she said she had received criticism for “hating trans,” which she denied.</p><p>“I think that I am here to extend love,” Cunningham said. “But I also think that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men.”</p><p>Since the All-Star break, groups advocating to exclude transgender women from women’s sports have rallied outside Fever road games.</p><p><b>Amy Sousa</b>, who helped organize the first rally in Seattle, said she hadn’t ever watched the WNBA but now wants to support Cunningham.</p><p>“This whole thing has taken off,” she said. ”We’re here to be completely pro women, pro girl. Our basic stance is that women and girls sports need to be designated, as science says, on the basis of sex.”</p><p>Across Madison, others came specifically to support transgender athletes.</p><p>“Youth sports saved my life,” said one long-time Sky fan, who asked not to be named. “It’s hard enough feeling like a kid who feels different than everyone else. Not having a space in sports would have been so harmful to me.</p><p>“Which young girls is Cunningham trying to protect, and from who? I think that young girls in sports need protection from a lot of other things. There are so many trans kids who need to be lifted up and not torn down.”</p><p>They noted cyberbullying and ACL injuries as two things young girls actually need protection from.</p><p><b>WNBPA weighs in</b></p><p>The players union addressed the debate Friday, saying: “Hate, abuse, and demonization of any person or group of people, including transgender people, only fuel fear, division, and harm. We will continue to have hard conversations. But we will not be used as political pawns.”</p><p>WNBPA secretary <b>Elizabeth Williams</b> told the Sun-Times that especially when it comes to the conversation around trans athletes, people try to use WNBA players to advance their agendas.</p><p>“We just want to make sure that we’re recentering the focus back on protecting Title IX,” Williams said. “Protecting girls in sport. That’s always been our priority.”</p><p><b>Fouling around </b></p><p>Inside the arena, Sky guard <b>DiJonai Carrington</b> was ejected for a Flagrant 2 foul on Cunningham, and <b>Natasha Cloud</b> received a technical in the fourth quarter.</p><p><b>Caitlin Clark</b> was assessed a technical in the third quarter that would have triggered a one-game suspension. The WNBA rescinded it after the game.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: DiJonai Carrington ejected after hard foul on Sophie Cunningham as Sky fall to Fever
entries.summary: <p>It was a jumbled affair at the United Center, even by the standards of this <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> season.</p><p>Outside the arena, dueling protests had formed around Fever guard Sophie Cunningham’s recent comments opposing transgender women participating in women’s sports. Inside, a game moved from Wintrust Arena to accommodate a bigger crowd felt more like Gainbridge Fieldhouse West than a home game for the Sky.</p><p>And in the middle of it all, the Sky lost another close one, 90-86.</p><p>The Fever gave their traveling fans plenty to cheer about early. Caitlin Clark put on a show, making all the right reads and hitting 5-of-6 from deep. The Sky looked sluggish, missing layups and offering little resistance.</p><p>Then DiJonai Carrington checked in.</p><p>Carrington, who missed the first half of the season recovering from foot surgery, has changed the Sky’s energy since returning. She did it almost immediately Saturday, scoring eight points in three minutes and helping turn an early deficit into a lead.</p><p>But it didn’t last.</p><p>Cunningham broke free in transition, and Carrington chased her down from behind. Carrington went for the block but caught Cunningham across the head and neck, sending her hard to the floor.</p><p>Cunningham popped back up and gave Carrington a little shove. Words followed before teammates and security separated them.</p><p>After review, Carrington was assessed a Flagrant 2 and ejected. Cunningham was not given a technical. Officials later said they “deemed her reaction to the severity of the contact to be acceptable.”</p><p>Minutes later, Carrington posted “WHITE PRIVILEGE” on Threads and tagged the Fever.</p><p>Neither coach thought the foul was intentional. Fever coach Stephanie White, who coached Carrington in Connecticut, and Sky coach Tyler Marsh both said they saw Carrington making a play on the ball.</p><p>Cunningham took the opposite stance.</p><p>She said she “absolutely” believed Carrington fouled her intentionally, adding that she has “no beef” with Carrington but believes she has “some pent-up stuff.”</p><p>“So, get your s— off,” Cunningham said. “That’s fine. I can take it.”</p><p>There is some history here, although not directly between Cunningham and Carrington.</p><p>One of the moments that helped build Cunningham’s reputation as Clark’s “enforcer” came last season against the Sun. After Clark and current Sky guard Jacy Sheldon, longtime Big Ten rivals at Iowa and Ohio State, tangled earlier in the game, Cunningham later put Sheldon in a headlock during a fastbreak.</p><p>Cunningham acknowledged the parallel, but balked at Carrington getting involved.</p><p>“I did that last year. Yeah, it’s intentional, but [Carrington] wasn’t even on the team,” Cunningham said. “She has no reason to be doing any of that… Good way to get her kicked out.”</p><p>“I do know when people play the Fever, we’re nationally televised, there’s a lot of eyes on us,” Cunningham said. “People just want attention. That’s her just trying to get attention.”</p><p>Asked about Carrington’s “WHITE PRIVILEGE” post, Cunningham dismissed race as a factor.</p><p>“This has nothing to do with race,” Cunningham said. “Last year I did the same thing. I got kicked out, as I deserved to be kicked out. There’s no reason to even play that card.”</p><p>The exchange only added to the controversy already swirling around Cunningham, whose comments about transgender women in sports had followed the Fever from city to city.</p><p>“I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men,” Cunningham said in a recent ESPN interview.</p><p>She has since called that position “common sense.” Her comments have spurred rallies outside Fever games from groups such as XX-XY Athletics, which argues that it is “unfair and dangerous to allow males to compete in girls’ and women’s sports.”</p><p>There was also a counterprotest in support of transgender athletes outside the United Center on Saturday.</p><p>Marsh said none of it gave the Sky any more “juice” than usual. With their playoff chances dwindling, he said their focus remains on basketball.</p><p>“We’re just locked in on hoops, really,” Sheldon said. “We come to every game kind of the same, locked in on the scouting report, what we want to get done and ultimately try to win and play good basketball. So that was just our focus. There was no conversation outside of that.”</p><p>One thing that kept the Sky from playing their best basketball was losing Carrington early.</p><p>They were already without leading scorer Sydney Taylor, sidelined by a groin injury. Then they lost one of their best perimeter defenders and most aggressive shot creators after three minutes.</p><p>In a game decided by four points, that hurt.</p>

entries.summary: <p>A fire in an abandoned building in Little Village Saturday night was extinguished in about an hour, according to Chicago police and fire officials.</p><p>Police and firefighters responded to the fire about 7:30 p.m. in the 2200 block of South Lawndale Avenue, police said. entries.title: White Sox add Hagen Smith and Tanner McDougal, beat Guardians to restore three-game AL Central lead
entries.summary: <p>Getting the call to the major leagues was an emotional moment for new <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> pitchers <b>Tanner McDougal</b> and <b>Hagen Smith</b>. But as two of the Sox’ top prospects, they understand their assignment is much more than being feel-good stories.</p><p>‘‘I’m excited to go out there and compete and hopefully help win a pennant back here,’’ said McDougal, the Sox’ No. 4 prospect, according to MLB Pipeline.</p><p>There’s still some time before the Sox can do that, but they gave themselves some breathing room in the American League Central race Saturday by beating the Guardians 6-3. The Sox snapped a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/07/white-sox-manager-will-venable-appears-to-make-one-of-the-gaffes-of-the-season-in-key-game-against-guardians" target="_blank" >season-high four-game losing streak</a> and restored their three-game lead over the Guardians and Twins in the division.</p><p>‘‘It’s obviously a very important series, so I’m really glad that we got to win this one,’’ said first baseman <b>Munetaka Murakami</b>, who homered in the Sox’ five-run sixth that overturned a 2-0 deficit. ‘‘We were in a bad losing streak right here, so it’s good to reset and then come back today with a win.’’</p><p>Neither McDougal nor Smith, the team’s No. 2 prospect, were used Saturday, but they will be relievers. Both have had injuries this season and were working out of the bullpen at Triple-A Charlotte despite having starting pedigrees.</p><p>And both will be tested in a race that might go down to the last days of the season.</p><p>‘‘It’s awesome,’’ Smith said. ‘‘To go out there and compete is the biggest thing for me. Love going out there and [competing] and [going] out there and [attacking] the hitters.’’</p><p>To make room for McDougal and Smith, the Sox sent left-hander <b>Noah Schultz</b> and right-hander <b>David Sandlin</b> to Charlotte. They also designated right-hander <b>Wikelman Gonzalez</b> for assignment.</p><h3>The Schultz plan</h3><p>Schultz will be a starter in the minors. Sox manager <b>Will Venable</b> said there are some mechanical issues Schultz needs to iron out.</p><p>Right-hander <b>Erick Fedde</b>, who was dropped from the rotation after the Sox acquired <b>Luis Castillo</b> from the Mariners at the trade deadline, is a candidate to make the next start in Schultz’s spot. Venable didn’t definitively anoint Fedde a starter again because the Sox still might need him out of the bullpen in the next few days.</p><h3>The gaffe</h3><p>Venable still wasn’t over his blunder Friday that forced Schultz from the game when he made a second mound visit in the first inning. Venable said he didn’t sleep well afterward, probably would lose sleep for a couple of more nights and wasn’t OK yet with what happened.</p><p>He also knew he needed to look forward.</p><p>‘‘That’s what this league is about: You’ve got to dust yourself off and get back up and go to battle,’’ Venable said. ‘‘So that’s what we’re going to do.’’</p>

entries.title: How Blackhawks rookie Anton Frondell is preparing to play center in the NHL
entries.summary: <p>Anton Frondell has an opportunity to be the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' first-line center, at least for the first month of the season during Connor Bedard's absence.</p><p>The 19-year-old Swedish forward personally hasn't given much thought to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/26/projecting-blackhawks-lines-patrick-kane-bowen-byram-connor-bedard-frank-nazar" target="_blank" >what line</a> he will play on. But he has spent his entire summer thinking about and preparing for his new position.</p><p>His tryout at center at the end of last season came unexpectedly, since he had played exclusively on the wing for his Swedish club, Djurgardens. He <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/01/blackhawks-anton-frondell-video-breakdown-center-jonathan-toews" target="_blank" >showed promise</a> in his first 12 NHL games, nine of which were spent at center, by recording nine points. But he also struggled on faceoffs and missed some defensive assignments.</p><p>By the time the puck drops for the Hawks' 2026-27 season opener Sept. 29 at the Golden Knights, he should look more comfortable at center.</p><p>"You need to know the whole game and how to play the role in the middle," Frondell said Friday on the phone from Sweden, where he was driving home to a hearty pasta dinner.</p><p>"I'm trying to study it, watch a couple players and look deep into faceoffs and how to try to win more."</p><p>Panthers star Aleksander Barkov has long been Frondell's idol, so the fact he's one of the most dominant two-way centers in the world made him an obvious choice to feature in Frondell's video sessions this summer. Frondell also got to face Barkov on the ice for the first time in an exhibition game before the world championships in May.</p><p>At the dot, Frondell (who won only 30.2% of his faceoffs in those 12 games) has an extremely long way to go to catch Barkov (56.9% over his last two healthy seasons). But after studying Barkov, he thinks his sheer strength could be an advantage.</p><p>"Faceoffs is a lot of timing, a lot of reacting quick to when the puck drops, and then if you're strong and you have a lot of power in your faceoffs, you can win a lot of them," Frondell said. "That's a way for me to win more: with my power."</p><p>It's worth noting Frondell's weight has held steady at 209 pounds for the past year. Unlike many other Hawks forward prospects, he has already filled out his 6-1 frame and then some. He is undoubtedly a power forward, which makes him something of a unicorn within the Hawks' young core.</p><p>At his size, increasing quickness and explosiveness must be higher priorities, which Frondell realized upon joining the Hawks in March.</p><p>"[With] the style of hockey and the rink I'm used to — the Swedish size — the game is a little bit different, and I could see that right away when I got to play a couple NHL games," he said. </p><p>"[In Sweden], you can save your speed or use your glide a little bit. In the NHL, it felt like everything was tighter. As a center in the D-zone, you need to get out to the corner quick, then get back in front of the net, [then] maybe to the other corner."</p><p>During Frondell's 2024-25 draft year, his skating was considered a weakness, but the Hawks were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2025/07/13/blackhawks-anton-frondell-nhl-draft-prospects-marcus-kruger-johnny-oduya-sweden" target="_blank" >less concerned about it</a> than other teams because they could tell how hard he was working to improve it — and how steadily it was improving as a result.</p><p>That trend has continued this summer, which Frondell has spent doing sprints in the gym and then translating those movements onto the ice.</p><p>"I feel like when I'm at my top speed, I can use it," he said. "But I want to get into my speed faster so I can earn time and space in the first couple steps."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">🚨ANTON FRONDELL FIRST NHL GOAL🚨 <a href="https://t.co/8AEuLEIg74">pic.twitter.com/8AEuLEIg74</a></p>— Blackhawks on CHSN (@CHSN_Blackhawks) <a href="https://x.com/CHSN_Blackhawks/status/2039143453645295620?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">April 1, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>He certainly hasn't slacked training-wise. He took only about a week off after the world championships before resuming light skating with brothers William Eklund (Sharks) and Victor Eklund (Islanders), two close friends. </p><p>Then he ramped up his on-ice work with a group of players including Tom Willander (Canucks), a summer training partner for the last several years. </p><p>Since last week, Frondell — along with the Eklunds and Viggo Bjorck (Jets) — have been practicing with Djurgardens, whose first exhibition game is Thursday. The NHL-bound kids won't play in any games, but they will go through an entire training camp before NHL camps begin in September.</p><p>"For us, it's perfect," Frondell said. "When everything starts, we'll already have a feeling for team practice. [We'll have] been going into battles and all that stuff."</p><p>Bjorck, at the NHL draft combine in June, described Frondell as a "more calm version of Victor," and he is certainly low-strung and lighthearted for being such a competitive, driven person.</p><p>He's not fazed by much, including the lofty expectations for his official NHL rookie season: he's tied for fourth in preseason Calder Trophy odds, per FanDuel.</p><p>Perhaps Frondell's affinity for tennis contributes to that zen mindset. Tennis allows him to escape the hockey bubble, get outdoors and appreciate the simplicity when it's "just you and the racket," as he described last summer.</p><p>Both his dad, Henrik, and his older sister, Alva, played tennis competitively, and they still spend several hours each week dueling on a clay court near their summer house.</p><p>"It's just a fun thing to do and think about something else," Frondell said Friday. "And at the same time, getting some training [with] hand-eye [coordination] and footwork."</p><p>When the idea of soon becoming teammates with Patrick Kane pops into Frondell's head, though, some excitement does penetrate his easygoing attitude.</p><p>"Growing up, you watch every highlight of him, every YouTube video you could find, and now I have the chance to sit in the same room as him," he said. "It's pretty cool and nothing I thought I would ever do."</p><p>Kane has mentioned Frank Nazar as a possible linemate during Bedard's absence, and Kane and Nazar's chemistry from skating together this summer could be a point in Nazar's favor.</p><p>But Frondell's attentiveness to defense — even if his defensive execution and analytics didn't quite match his effort this spring — as well as his deadly shot and ability to protect the puck and hold off opponents could make sense next to Kane, too.</p><p>The Hawks will have time, albeit not a lot, to experiment with these combinations during camp. Frondell hopes to leap into that process with as little rust as possible.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Lifeline Thrown to Nephew Instead Weighs Down Relatives
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I suggested to my husband that he invite his nephew "Ryan" (age 26) to stay with us. Ryan definitely needed some male direction. He was homeless, jobless and didn't even know how to apply for a job. Ryan is not mentally challenged. He simply was never taught anything until he was thrown out on the street with no skills.</p><p>Once Ryan moved in, I realized just how big a mistake we had made. He got a job because a relative was able to get him hired without even so much as an interview. He doesn't make enough money to move out on his own. He sleeps all day and plays video games all night anytime he's not at work.</p><p>Ryan doesn't shower, doesn't do his own laundry and leaves dirty dishes all over the room he sleeps in. The room smells horrible. On top of that, my clothes closet is in that room. (There is no other option for my clothes.) I'm worried his body odor and dirty clothes will soon make all my clothes smell as well.</p><p>This was meant to be a temporary situation until Ryan had saved enough to get his own place. However, he makes no effort to save toward that end. I wouldn't intervene if it weren't that he is diminishing my quality of life. I was all in for helping him out, but I can no longer live under these conditions. My husband keeps saying he'll handle it but doesn't. It's not my place because Ryan is his relative. I'm in desperate need of your wisdom. — <i>SMELLY SITUATION</i></p><p><b>DEAR SMELLY SITUATION:</b> Ryan's parents did their son a terrible disservice by not teaching him survival skills so he could live independently. Because you chose to take him off the streets, that task now falls to you. I say "you" because your husband doesn't appear to have the backbone to address this. Both of you need to tell Ryan there are rules he must follow if he wants to continue living with you.</p><p>Show him how to put his clothes (and detergent) into a washing machine and to use the dryer. Tell him he must shower at least three times a week and use deodorant every day. No longer tolerate food in his room or dirty dishes left in the sink. He must eat in the dining area like a civilized person.</p><p>Also, set up a savings plan for what little money he earns so part of his paycheck can accumulate and he can finally move out on his own — even if it's with a roommate. If he learns the lessons that you teach him, someone may actually be willing to share quarters with him. I wish you luck. Nothing will change until you assert yourself.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My son and I have been estranged for three years. He wants nothing more to do with me. I do not expect to see him ever again. However, I still have items of his. Do I pack up the items and have them dropped off, or what? I'm not sure what to do. — <i>EX-MOTHER IN ARIZONA</i></p><p><b>DEAR EX-MOTHER:</b> If you are sure that your son is still living at the same address, box the items up and send them. That way, you can never be blamed for withholding anything from him.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>
